result: Population-level cortical asymmetries are highly consistent across seven independent datasets from four countries. Areal asymmetries show high spatial correlation (r=0.88-0.97) with leftward asymmetry in supramarginal gyrus/perisylvian regions and rightward asymmetry in cingulate, inferior parietal cortex, and STS. Thickness asymmetries show an anterior-posterior pattern with more variable spatial correlations (r=0.33-0.93), with consistent leftward asymmetry in cingulate, postcentral gyrus, and superior frontal cortex, and rightward asymmetry in STS, insula, and lingual gyrus.
evaluation: Claims C28-C35 provide converging evidence from multiple datasets showing replicable patterns of cortical asymmetry. The spatial correlation analyses (C28, C33) and overlapping effects across datasets (C29, C30, C34) demonstrate robust population-level asymmetries. The consistency of individual lateralization proportions across datasets (C35) further supports the reliability of these findings. The results are well-documented with quantitative metrics and visual evidence from Figure 1.

result: Areal asymmetry is predominantly stable across the lifespan from age 4 to 89 years. Asymmetry was strongly established by age ~4, with largely parallel trajectories for both leftward and rightward asymmetries throughout life. There was little indication of relative hemispheric differences during cortical development (4-30 years) or aging (30-89 years), and areal asymmetry was significantly different from zero across the entire lifespan in all clusters.
evaluation: Claims C2, C36-C38 are supported by longitudinal lifespan trajectory analyses using GAMMs in the LCBC sample (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplements). The parallel trajectories and early establishment of asymmetry by age 4 are clearly demonstrated. The statistical analyses confirm asymmetry is significantly different from zero across the lifespan, supporting the interpretation of developmental stability.

result: Thickness asymmetry grows during childhood and peaks in early adulthood (median age ~24.3 years). Homotopic trajectories were non-parallel, characterized by developmental increase in thickness asymmetry from age 4-30 through unequal rates of continuous thinning between hemispheres. In 10/20 clusters, developmental increase corresponded to a significant relative hemispheric difference in the rate of developmental thinning, with the thicker hemisphere thinning comparatively slower. Despite this growth, 95% of clusters exhibited small but significant asymmetry already by age ~4.
evaluation: Claims C3, C39-C43, C95 are supported by longitudinal trajectory analyses presented in Figures 3 and 4. The non-parallel trajectories, relative hemispheric differences in thinning rates, and age at peak asymmetry are quantitatively documented. The finding that asymmetry is already present at age 4 but continues to grow is well-supported by the GAMM analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).

result: Most clusters did not exhibit relative hemispheric differences in rates of cortical thinning during aging (30-89 years), except in regions overlapping with previous reports (e.g., mPFC). This fits with previous work showing aging-related loss in thickness asymmetry is specific to heteromodal regions vulnerable in aging.
evaluation: Claims C44, C104, C105 are supported by the relative aging trajectory analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and citations to prior work (Roe et al., 2021). The finding that most clusters do not show aging-related hemispheric differences is clearly documented, with exceptions noted in specific regions that overlap with previous analyses.

result: For areal asymmetry, a common covariance structure between asymmetries was detectable across datasets with correlation matrices correlating almost perfectly (r ≥ 0.97). The highest correlations reflected positive correlations between regions that are on average left-asymmetric and regions that are on average right-asymmetric. Opposite-direction areal asymmetries were more correlated if closer in cortex (geodesic distance), while same-direction asymmetries were not. These relationships could not be explained by brain size (ICV).
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by Mantel tests and interregional correlation analyses presented in Figure 5A and 5C. The replication across three independent datasets (LCBC, UKB, HCP) with high correlation coefficients provides strong evidence. The geodesic distance analysis and ICV control analysis further support the specificity of these relationships.

result: For thickness asymmetry, a common covariance structure replicated across datasets (Mantel test r=0.46-0.62). Higher leftward asymmetry in left-asymmetric regions corresponded to more leftward asymmetry in right-asymmetric regions, and vice versa. PCA revealed PC1 explained 21.9% of variance in UKB, and there was a correlation of r=-0.61 between mean asymmetry across all leftward vs. rightward clusters. This indicates individuals may tend towards either leftward asymmetry, rightward asymmetry, or symmetry globally across the cortex, irrespective of the region-specific average direction of asymmetry.
evaluation: Claims C50-C54, C110 are supported by correlation analyses, Mantel tests, and PCA presented in Figure 5B, 5D, and supplementary figures. The pattern is most clear in UKB but replicates in LCBC and HCP. The interpretation of global directional tendencies is supported by the detailed inspection of correlations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and the PCA results.

result: Areal asymmetry is low-moderately heritable with maximum h2SNP approximately 19% in anterior insula. Global areal asymmetry heritability was substantially lower (h2SNP=7%, h2twin=16%) than hemispheric measures (h2SNP ~67%, h2twin ~92%). Four areal asymmetries showed significant twin-based heritability in HCP (19-27%), all of which were also significant in SNP-based analyses (8-19%). SNP-based analyses revealed 9/14 (64%) areal asymmetry clusters exhibited significant heritability.
evaluation: Claims C4, C55-C59 are supported by heritability analyses using both SNP-based (UKB) and twin-based (HCP) methods. The convergence of results across methods and the specific identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region (h2SNP=18.6%) provide strong evidence. The contrast between high hemispheric heritability and low asymmetry heritability is well-documented.

result: Thickness asymmetry exhibits low or absent heritability. Only 3/20 (15%) thickness asymmetries exhibited significant SNP-based heritability (h2SNP=3-7%), and two robust asymmetries survived correction in twin-based analyses (rightward STS and lingual gyrus). Cluster-wise heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using a SNP-based approach (β=-1.1, p=0.0008) but not a twin-based approach.
evaluation: Claims C6, C60-C62 are supported by heritability analyses presented in the manuscript and Supplementary file 1I. The low heritability of thickness asymmetry is consistently demonstrated across both SNP-based and twin-based methods, with statistical comparison confirming significantly lower heritability for thickness vs. area asymmetry in SNP-based analyses.

result: Cortex-wide heritability analysis revealed consistent patterns for areal asymmetry across SNP- and twin-based methods. In HCP, 69 parcels survived FDR-correction, 84% of which were also significant in SNP-based analysis. In UKB, 267 (53%) parcels exhibited significant SNP-based heritability. Higher heritability was observed in anterior insula, SMG, Sylvian fissure, STS, calcarine sulcus, cingulate, medial and orbitofrontal cortex, and fusiform, with spatial correlation r=0.46 between SNP- and twin-based maps. Maximum SNP-heritability was observed in anterior insula (16.4%).
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by cortex-wide heritability analyses presented in Figure 6A. The convergence of results across SNP- and twin-based methods, the high proportion of significant parcels, and the consistent spatial pattern provide strong evidence. The identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region is well-documented.

result: For thickness asymmetry, cortex-wide heritability was low and inconsistent between methods. Only 15 parcels survived FDR-correction in twin-based analysis, 7 of which were also significant in SNP-based analysis. Significant SNP-heritability was observed in only 11% (57) of parcels. There was little visual overlap in twin- and SNP-based heritability patterns (spatial correlation r=0.24). Cortex-wide heritability estimates were significantly lower for thickness asymmetry than for area using both SNP-based (β=-0.71, p<2.2e-16) and twin-based approaches (β=-0.33, p=1.08e-7).
evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by cortex-wide heritability analyses presented in Figure 6B. The low heritability, limited spatial extent of significant parcels, poor agreement between methods, and statistical comparison with areal asymmetry all provide converging evidence for low heritability of thickness asymmetry.

result: For areal asymmetry, large SNP-based genetic correlations explained several phenotypic correlations, including high correlations between leftward SMG/perisylvian and rightward lateral parietal cortex (rGSNP=0.83), leftward superior frontal cortex and rightward cingulate (rGSNP=0.82), and leftward anterior temporal/parahippocampal and rightward lateral parietal cortex (rGSNP=0.68). Two twin-based genetic correlations survived FDR-correction, including replication of the SMG/perisylvian - lateral parietal cortex correlation (rGtwin=1.0). For thickness asymmetry, only one post-corrected significant SNP-based genetic correlation was found (rGSNP=0.68).
evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by genetic correlation analyses presented in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The convergence of SNP-based and twin-based results for areal asymmetry, particularly the replication of the SMG/perisylvian - lateral parietal cortex correlation, provides strong evidence. The contrast with thickness asymmetry (only one significant correlation) is well-documented.

result: Higher areal asymmetry in the largest leftward cluster (SMG/perisylvian) was significantly associated with better general cognitive ability (β=0.03, p=7.4e-7) in UK Biobank. This association was far from the correction threshold and retained significance in the non-imputed subset.
evaluation: Claims C7 and C77 are supported by association analyses in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7. The effect size is small but statistically robust, surviving Bonferroni correction and replication in the non-imputed subset. The authors appropriately note the small effect size and the association is with the most consistently lateralized region in humans (~94% of individuals show leftward asymmetry).

result: Reduced leftward areal asymmetry in anterior insula and thickness asymmetry along postcentral gyrus was evident in left-handers. Males typically exhibited slightly stronger areal asymmetry in large clusters (e.g., leftward SMG/perisylvian and temporal pole; rightward inferior parietal and superior frontal) but reduced asymmetry in mPFC. For thickness, males exhibited more rightward asymmetry in STS and posterior insula, more leftward asymmetry in superior frontal cortex, but reduced rightward asymmetry in entorhinal cortex and anterior insula.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by association analyses in UK Biobank data presented in Figure 7 and Supplementary file 1J-K. The handedness findings are consistent with prior work (Sha et al., 2021a). The sex effects are small but statistically significant and show region-specific patterns. All effects survived Bonferroni correction.

result: Areal asymmetry is developmentally stable and arises early in life through genetic but mainly subject-specific stochastic effects. Adult-like patterns of lateralization were strongly established before age ~4, indicating areal asymmetry traces back further and does not primarily emerge through later cortical expansion. This may align with evidence indicating areal asymmetry may be primarily determined in utero and fits with the principle that the primary microstructural basis of cortical area is determined in prenatal life. While heritability of either hemisphere was high, areal asymmetry heritability was only moderate at best, suggesting genetic but primarily subject-specific stochastic effects underlie its formation.
evaluation: Claims C8, C87, C90-C93, C119, C121 represent an integrated interpretation of multiple findings: lifespan stability (C2, C36-C38), low-moderate heritability (C4, C55-C59), and early establishment by age 4. This interpretation is well-supported by the data and consistent with prior literature on prenatal brain development (Li et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2023; Rakic, 1995). The authors appropriately acknowledge that work linking prenatal and childhood trajectories is needed to affirm this interpretation (C87).

result: Childhood developmental growth shapes thickness asymmetry and may lead to directional variability of global thickness lateralization in the population. Developmental trajectories suggest differentiation of the cortex occurs with respect to thickness asymmetry in development, possibly suggesting it may be more amenable to experience-dependent change. Thickness asymmetry growth may suggest hemispheric differences in the developmental optimization of cortical networks at least partly shaped by childhood experience. This raises the possibility thickness asymmetry may be a marker of ontogenetic hemispheric specialization within neurocognitive networks. However, this is speculative, and intervention approaches are needed to experimentally test plasticity of thickness asymmetry in humans.
evaluation: Claims C9, C88, C96-C99, C113, C114, C122 represent a speculative interpretation of the combined findings of developmental growth trajectories, low heritability, and global interrelations of thickness asymmetry. While the data support developmental growth and low heritability, the interpretation that this reflects experience-dependent plasticity is speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this speculation (C99) and note that intervention approaches are needed to test this hypothesis. The interpretation is plausible but not directly demonstrated by the data.

result: For areal asymmetry, most asymmetries were either not or only weakly correlated, fitting with a multifaceted view and contrasting views emphasizing a single factor controlling cerebral lateralization. However, several regions wherein areal asymmetry reliably correlated within individuals were identified, showing the variance in cortical asymmetries is not always dissociable. Several of these were underpinned by high asymmetry-asymmetry SNP-based genetic correlations, illustrating some lateralizations in surface area exhibit coordinated genetic development.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by interregional correlation analyses (Figure 5A) and genetic correlation analyses (Figure 6C). The finding that most asymmetries are weakly correlated but some show strong correlations is well-documented. The genetic correlations provide mechanistic insight into the coordinated development of specific asymmetries.

result: The global interrelation of thickness asymmetry may be in broad agreement with the notion that some lateralized genetic-developmental programs may trigger lateralization in either direction or lose their directional bias through environmental interaction. As thickness asymmetry seems established at but minimal from birth, genetic effects may determine the average region-specific hemispheric bias in the population, but later developmental change may subsequently confer major increases upon its directional variance.
evaluation: Claims C111 and C112 are speculative interpretations of the thickness asymmetry findings. While the data support global interrelation, low heritability, and developmental growth, the specific interpretation regarding directional bias and environmental interaction is not directly tested. The interpretation is plausible and consistent with prior theories (Francks, 2015) but remains speculative.

result: Areal asymmetry in anterior insula is the most heritable asymmetry yet reported with genomic methods (h2SNP ~19%), notably higher than in a recent report (<5%). Highest SNP and twin-based heritability for areal asymmetry was found in regions constituting the earliest emerging cortical asymmetries in utero (anterior insula, STS, PT, medial occipital cortex, parahippocampal gyrus). The effects agree with and elaborate on two previous genetic explorations and reports of heritable areal asymmetry in handedness-associated clusters. Since asymmetry here emerges early in utero and is by far the most heritable, this ontogenetically foundational region of cortex may be fruitful for understanding genetic-developmental mechanisms influencing laterality.
evaluation: Claims C115-C118, C130 are supported by heritability analyses (Figure 6A) and citations to prior literature on prenatal brain development (Dubois et al., 2010; Habas et al., 2012; Kasprian et al., 2011; Hill et al., 2010). The identification of anterior insula as the most heritable region is well-documented, and the comparison to prior work (Sha et al., 2021a) demonstrates improvement in the approach. The interpretation regarding genetic-developmental mechanisms is reasonable given the convergence of heritability and prenatal development findings.

result: These results support a differentiation between early-life (i.e., before age ~4) and later developmental factors in shaping areal and thickness asymmetry, respectively.
evaluation: Claim C124 is a summary interpretation supported by the combined findings of lifespan stability and low-moderate heritability for areal asymmetry (C2, C4, C36-C38, C55-C59) versus developmental growth and low heritability for thickness asymmetry (C3, C6, C39-C43, C60-C62). This differentiation is a major conclusion of the study and is well-supported by the data.

result: The vertex-wise analysis of cortical asymmetries that reproduce across adult cohorts replicates and completes a recent low-resolution meta-analysis and can serve as a high-fidelity phenotype for future brain asymmetry studies. The marked consistency across samples suggests consensus may now be reached regarding cortical asymmetry phenotypes in humans. The high overlap in effects between seven datasets from four countries suggests these results likely apply universally. This evident consensus suggests genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization with respect to both area and apparent thickness in humans.
evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are interpretations of the population-level asymmetry findings (C28-C35) in relation to prior literature. The high consistency across seven international datasets provides strong evidence for the universality of these asymmetry patterns. The interpretation that genetic-developmental programs regulate mean brain lateralization is supported by the consistency of patterns across samples, though the low heritability findings (C85) suggest these programs may have reached population fixation.

result: The genetic findings suggest cortical asymmetries may have reached population fixation, as heritability of even optimally delineated asymmetry measures was generally low. This indicates either subject-specific stochastic mechanisms in early neurodevelopment or later developmental influences primarily determine cortical asymmetry.
evaluation: Claims C85 and C86 are interpretations of the heritability findings (C4, C6, C55-C62). The low heritability despite consistent population-level patterns is well-documented. The interpretation that this indicates population fixation or subject-specific stochastic/developmental influences is reasonable, though the relative contributions of these factors remain to be determined.

result: The findings agree with work finding a similar left-right thickness asymmetry pattern shows rapid longitudinal increase in the first years of life, particularly in mPFC. As rapid asymmetry differentiation spanning childhood and adolescence was observed in most prefrontal regions and others, these findings extend earlier findings in neonates. Likely, longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling was critical to capture early developmental growth in thickness asymmetry within a lifespan perspective. As prefrontal thickness asymmetry seems particularly vulnerable in some neurodevelopmental disorders, aging, and Alzheimer's disease, these trajectories provide a useful normative reference regarding the timing of expected brain change in development.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are interpretations of the thickness asymmetry developmental findings (C3, C39-C43) in relation to prior literature (Li et al., 2015; Postema et al., 2019; Roe et al., 2021). The agreement with prior work and the extension to childhood and adolescence are well-supported. The interpretation regarding the importance of longitudinal data and nonlinear modelling is reasonable given the complexity of the trajectories. The clinical relevance is supported by citations to prior literature.

result: Since interhemispheric anatomy in the SMG/perisylvian region is likely related to brain torque, the association with cognitive ability may agree with work suggesting torque relates to cognitive outcomes. That ~94% of humans exhibit leftward asymmetry in this region suggests tightly regulated genetic-developmental programs control its lateralized direction in humans. This result may suggest disruptions in areal lateralization early in life are associated with cognitive deficits detectable in later life as small effects in big data. While speculative, this may also agree with evidence that differences in general cognitive ability that show high lifespan stability relate primarily to areal phenotypes formed early in life.
evaluation: Claims C125-C128 are speculative interpretations of the cognitive association finding (C7, C77). While the association is statistically robust, the interpretation regarding brain torque, disruptions in early life, and cognitive deficits is speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this speculation (C128) and cite relevant prior literature (Toga and Thompson, 2003; LeMay, 1976; Kong, 2019; Zhao et al., 2021; Deary et al., 2004; Walhovd et al., 2016; Rakic, 1995; Fjell et al., 2019). The interpretation is plausible but not directly demonstrated.

result: Anterior insula lies within a left-lateralized functional language network, and its structural asymmetry may relate to language lateralization in which left-handers show increased atypicality. Less leftward somatosensory thickness asymmetry in left-handers echoes a recent report and fits a scenario whereby thickness asymmetries may be partly shaped through use-dependent plasticity and detectable through group-level hemispheric specializations of function. Still, the small effects show cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness. Associations with other factors typically assumed important were similarly small, and mostly compatible with prior reports. Possibly, differences in sample median age and potential sex-differences in brain decline may underlie some inconsistencies.
evaluation: Claims C129, C131-C134 are interpretations of the handedness and sex association findings (C78-C80) in relation to prior literature. The associations are statistically significant but small, as appropriately noted. The interpretation regarding language lateralization and use-dependent plasticity is supported by citations to prior literature (Labache et al., 2019; Chiarello et al., 2013; Biduła and Króliczak, 2015; Keller et al., 2011; Wiberg et al., 2019; Mazoyer et al., 2014; Westerhausen et al., 2006; Carey and Johnstone, 2014; Sha et al., 2021a). The acknowledgment that cortical asymmetry cannot predict individual handedness is appropriate given the small effect sizes.
